AWS AIP-C01 Architecture Decision Guide

Use this AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01) recap to practise defending architecture decisions before the exam. Use Northstar Assistant throughout: a customer asks a question, the application retrieves permitted evidence, Bedrock generates a response, and controlled tools may act on it. Start with the AI learning pages for concepts and the AWS service reference for implementation details.

Blueprint checked: 6 October 2026. The five domain weights are 31% / 26% / 20% / 12% / 11%. Focus on integrating foundation models into production applications, including customization deployment and lifecycle controls. Model development/training and advanced ML are outside the exam’s stated scope; the model diagnostics here provide supporting context. Use the current AWS exam guide as the authority; study shortcuts are starting hypotheses.

0. GenAI Mindmap

Start with the requirements, then compare models using approved representative data. The model lifecycle selects, optionally customizes, evaluates, deploys, and monitors the model. Prompt engineering and RAG shape the runtime context. The four supporting pillars apply throughout. Select a map box to study its purpose and decision boundary, then choose a related situation. Prompt → RAG → fine-tune is a starting heuristic, subject to the requirement and measured results.

ARCHITECTURE BEFORE SERVICESOne system. Find the layer that owns the problem.

Prepare knowledge, assemble context, invoke the model, and verify the outcome. The model lifecycle selects, customizes, evaluates, and deploys the model. Prompt and RAG supply runtime context; the four pillars apply throughout.

Principles first; services replace the descriptions inside the same boxes.
Data / lifecycle flowRuntime requestLifecycle inputs / deploymentMonitoring feedback
Diagnose backwards. Find the boundary.

Select a map layer to understand its purpose, then explore a related situation and inspect the evidence.

Select a box in the map to study its purpose and related situations.

The static checkpoints below keep the same scenarios, evidence, and decision rules available without JavaScript.

RAG / evidence → answer

Find where approved evidence first disappeared, changed meaning, became inaccessible, or stopped supporting the answer.

SourceSituation

The assistant gives an outdated policy, or the required fact is not present even in the current original document.

What this means

The original document or business record is the authority for the fact the assistant needs.

Inspect the evidence

Compare the authoritative object, version, permission, and required passage with the failing question.

Decision boundary / trap

If the fact is absent or stale at source, downstream ranking cannot create it.

PreprocessSituation

A scan or transcript looks readable, but a table column, exception, speaker turn, or identifier has disappeared.

What this means

Preprocessing converts the original document, image, or audio into a usable representation without losing its meaning.

Inspect the evidence

Compare extraction/transcription output against the original tables, qualifiers, and identifiers.

Decision boundary / trap

Repair missing meaning before changing vector size or model weights.

ParseSituation

The extracted text mixes table cells or drops headings, so the chunker receives an incomplete or misleading passage.

What this means

Parsing extracts text and structure, including table relationships, headings, and exceptions, before chunking.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect the actual text and structure entering the chunker.

Decision boundary / trap

An extraction defect is earlier than a chunk-boundary defect.

ChunkingSituation

The answer is split from its exception or section heading. A retrieved fragment looks correct but changes meaning without its neighbours.

What this means

A chunk is a small searchable unit of a document. Its boundaries determine which facts and conditions stay together.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect the units containing the answer and its exceptions; check boundaries and overlap.

Decision boundary / trap

Use a supported chunking strategy or ingestion extension before replacing RAG.

MetadataSituation

A passage has the wrong version or missing access tags; retrieval may return stale evidence or exclude permitted content.

What this means

Metadata describes a chunk: its source, version, identifiers, and which callers may access it.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect source/version identifiers and trusted ACL fields attached to each required chunk.

Decision boundary / trap

Similarity cannot compensate for missing access or freshness metadata.

Document embeddingSituation

Known paraphrases do not find their relevant documents, or the index rejects vectors after an embedding configuration change.

What this means

A document embedding is a numeric representation used to find passages with related meaning.

Inspect the evidence

Check embedding model, dimensions/configuration, and measured recall on this corpus.

Decision boundary / trap

Matching dimensions are necessary, but the embedding spaces must also be compatible.

IndexSituation

The source contains the answer, but its corresponding current chunk is missing from the searchable index.

What this means

The index is the searchable copy of your chunks, vectors, and metadata. It can differ from the original source.

Inspect the evidence

Confirm the exact current chunk/vector/metadata exists and synchronization succeeded.

Decision boundary / trap

Missing chunk → investigate ingestion; a reranker cannot recreate it.

Query / scopeSituation

Searching for an exact equipment ID returns similar products, or trusted access filters unexpectedly exclude the required document.

What this means

The retrieval query carries the question, exact identifiers, and trusted access scope used to search the corpus.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect the real query, meaningful IDs, trusted tenant scope, and filters sent downstream.

Decision boundary / trap

Do not remove exact identifiers or loosen authorization to improve recall.

Query embeddingSituation

Retrieval breaks or degrades after only the query embedding model or dimensions change; indexed documents still use the old settings.

What this means

A query embedding represents the question numerically so it can be compared with document embeddings.

Inspect the evidence

Compare query-vector generation with the indexed document-vector contract.

Decision boundary / trap

Changing the query model alone does not migrate the index.

CandidatesSituation

The right passage exists in the index and is permitted for this caller, but the initial search never returns it.

What this means

Candidates are the passages the initial search actually returns. Only these passages are available to a downstream reranker.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect the permitted pre-rerank candidates and whether the required evidence is present.

Decision boundary / trap

Indexed and permitted but absent here → investigate search/filtering/recall.

RerankingSituation

The right passage was found, but less relevant passages rank above it. The answer may use the wrong evidence after selection.

What this means

A reranker changes the order of passages already found by search, so the most useful evidence is selected first.

Inspect the evidence

Compare before/after ordering, candidate input, top-k, and any removed relevant passages.

Decision boundary / trap

Present but poorly ordered → ranking; absent from input → upstream.

Context selectionSituation

The right passage is retrieved and ranked well, but it or its exception is removed to fit the model’s context budget.

What this means

Context selection chooses which retrieved passages fit into the model request, including necessary conditions and source references.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect final passages, parent context, qualifiers, citations, and token-budget pruning.

Decision boundary / trap

A good candidate can still be lost before it reaches the model.

PromptSituation

The needed evidence reaches the model, yet the answer ignores a condition, follows document instructions, or answers a different task.

What this means

The prompt is the actual assembled request: instructions, the user question, evidence, and any conversation history.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect the exact assembled messages, source separation, task rules, and context truncation.

Decision boundary / trap

Correct evidence plus unclear instructions is not solved by another vector database.

ModelSituation

The verified request is complete and clear, but this model repeatedly fails the task while a suitable baseline handles it.

What this means

The model generates an answer from the context and settings it actually receives.

Inspect the evidence

Compare outputs on the same verified context with the baseline and actual generation settings.

Decision boundary / trap

Only blame model capability after validating the input and output contract.

Answer / validationSituation

The answer sounds plausible, but its claims are unsupported, its citations do not justify them, or it misses the requested result.

What this means

The delivered result must satisfy the user’s request and be checked against evidence or the authoritative business outcome.

Inspect the evidence

Compare individual claims and citations against supplied evidence and the user requirement.

Decision boundary / trap

A valid citation or JSON shape is not proof of faithfulness or correctness.

Prompt / model answer quality

First define what a correct answer means. Choose a suitable model, supply clear instructions and relevant context, then generate and validate. Output checks verify both format and the original task rules; valid JSON alone is insufficient.

Task definitionSituation

Similar examples receive inconsistent categories because nobody defined where one label ends and another begins.

What this means

Task definition states exactly what to decide or produce, including the meaning of labels and boundary cases.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect label meanings, output requirements, ambiguity, and representative boundary cases.

Decision boundary / trap

A persona does not define missing business rules.

Model / task fitSituation

The model struggles with the task or modality even on clear representative inputs; prompt changes do not resolve the limitation.

What this means

Model selection means choosing a supported model that meets the actual task, quality, modality, latency, and cost requirements.

Inspect the evidence

Compare baseline performance, supported modality, context budget, and task requirements.

Decision boundary / trap

A public benchmark or larger model is not proof of task fit.

InstructionsSituation

The assistant invents an answer when evidence is missing or treats instructions inside a retrieved document as authoritative.

What this means

System instructions describe the task rules, authority boundaries, and how to handle insufficient or untrusted information.

Inspect the evidence

Check instruction priority, untrusted-source separation, refusal/escalation rules, and examples.

Decision boundary / trap

Prompt instructions cannot replace deterministic authorization.

Template versionSituation

A tested prompt works offline, but the deployed application renders different instructions, variables, or examples.

What this means

A prompt template is the reusable, versioned structure into which the application inserts task-specific inputs.

Inspect the evidence

Compare the evaluated template/variables with the deployed version and rendered payload.

Decision boundary / trap

A saved prompt version is not necessarily the version actually invoked.

EvidenceSituation

The answer misses a current private fact because the supplied passages never contained that fact or its qualifying condition.

What this means

Retrieved knowledge is the permitted source evidence included in the request to answer a question.

Inspect the evidence

Verify the selected knowledge contains the required facts and qualifications.

Decision boundary / trap

Missing current facts usually require evidence, not style fine-tuning.

History / stateSituation

The assistant forgets an earlier user fact because the relevant turn or application state was not included in the current request.

What this means

Conversation context is the relevant earlier discussion and application state explicitly supplied with the current request.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect included turns, authoritative state, permission scope, and trimming.

Decision boundary / trap

An inference API does not automatically retain every earlier turn.

Generation settingsSituation

The answer ends mid-sentence, stops at an unexpected string, or changes after deployment despite apparently identical instructions.

What this means

Generation settings control limits and behavior such as output length, stop sequences, and sampling. They do not establish factual truth.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect actual token limits, stop sequences, sampling, template, and model/API settings.

Decision boundary / trap

Cut-off output differs from hallucination; low temperature is not a truth guarantee.

Output contractSituation

The response fits the JSON schema but assigns the wrong category, invents a fact, or represents an invalid business action.

What this means

The delivered result must satisfy the user’s request and be checked against evidence or the authoritative business outcome.

Inspect the evidence

Check semantic correctness, factual support, schema, and actual business outcome separately.

Decision boundary / trap

Valid JSON can still encode an incorrect or unauthorized action.

Fine-tuning / training quality

Work from held-out task behavior back through the artifact, training configuration, records, and adaptation choice. Loss is evidence, not the final goal.

Base model / baselineSituation

The tuned model does not outperform the original model on the real task, or the selected base does not support the needed method.

What this means

Model selection means choosing a supported model that meets the actual task, quality, modality, latency, and cost requirements.

Inspect the evidence

Compare representative tasks with the untuned model and supported customization methods.

Decision boundary / trap

Fine-tuning is not automatically better than a suitable baseline.

Adaptation choiceSituation

Weight changes fail to fix frequently changing facts or ambiguous instructions because those gaps required evidence or clearer task rules.

What this means

Adaptation chooses what needs changing: instructions, retrieved facts, model behavior, or domain learning.

Inspect the evidence

State whether the gap is instructions, changing facts, stable behavior, or domain adaptation.

Decision boundary / trap

Prompting, RAG, supervised tuning, and continued pre-training solve different gaps.

Splits / lineageSituation

Evaluation looks excellent on familiar examples but collapses on genuinely new cases or an underrepresented user group.

What this means

Dataset splits separate training examples, tuning/validation examples, and independent final tests. Lineage records where each version came from.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect dataset versions, provenance, duplicates, leakage, and representative critical cohorts.

Decision boundary / trap

Training and final test data must remain independent.

Records / labelsSituation

The tuned model learns inconsistent answers—for example, equivalent inputs are labeled “approve” in one record and “reject” in another.

What this means

A training record pairs an input with the expected output or label. A label is the answer the model is being taught to produce.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect model-specific format, input/output alignment, labels, and sensitive content.

Decision boundary / trap

More incorrectly labeled examples can reinforce the defect.

Training configurationSituation

Training becomes unstable or the model ignores important parts of examples after a learning-rate, length, or format change.

What this means

Training configuration specifies how learning runs: supported method/base, data format, sequence length, learning rate, epochs, and batches.

Inspect the evidence

Compare supported base/method, tokenizer, length/truncation, learning rate, epochs, and batch settings.

Decision boundary / trap

A configuration change must be evaluated; more epochs is not a universal fix.

Training executionSituation

The job fails, produces no usable artifact, or trains on a different dataset/configuration than the release was intended to use.

What this means

Fine-tuning trains a supported model on task examples to change learned behavior; it is separate from supplying facts through RAG.

Inspect the evidence

Check job status, actual configuration/data, permissions, logs, and produced artifact identity.

Decision boundary / trap

A completed job proves execution, not the desired behavior.

Learning curvesSituation

Training error keeps falling while validation error or unseen-task failures increase: the model fits training examples without improving generalization.

What this means

Learning curves show how training and, where available, validation error change as training progresses.

Inspect the evidence

Compare available training/validation curves with held-out outputs and critical cohorts.

Decision boundary / trap

Improving training loss with worsening validation may indicate overfitting; also check data/split defects.

Checkpoint selectionSituation

The last saved model performs worse on new examples than an earlier checkpoint or the original baseline.

What this means

A checkpoint is a saved training artifact. Different checkpoints can generalize differently even within the same training run.

Inspect the evidence

Compare candidate checkpoints with the baseline using independent task and safety gates.

Decision boundary / trap

The final epoch or lowest training loss is not automatically the best checkpoint.

Held-out evaluationSituation

Average scores improve, but a critical safety case, task type, or user group regresses on independent examples.

What this means

Held-out evaluation tests a candidate on representative examples it was not trained or tuned to memorize.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect correctness, safety, task success, regressions, and relevant latency/cost.

Decision boundary / trap

A critical regression blocks promotion even if average quality improves.

Approved artifactSituation

The approved version does not match the artifact that passed evaluation, or the release lacks a clear compatible rollback target.

What this means

Artifact registration and approval record which version may be released. They do not perform the live deployment.

Inspect the evidence

Check exactly which artifact/configuration passed the gate and was approved.

Decision boundary / trap

Approval does not deploy it.

Live identitySituation

The candidate passes offline tests, but production still behaves like the old model or uses different inference settings.

What this means

Live verification checks which model, adapter, prompt, and route actually serve a real application request.

Inspect the evidence

Send an attributed smoke request through the real route; compare with the offline candidate.

Decision boundary / trap

If offline passes but live fails, inspect routing/version/serving before retraining.

Production behaviorSituation

Quality falls after release for real users, particularly on inputs or cohorts unlike those in the evaluation set.

What this means

Production monitoring connects real task outcomes and failures to the versions and user groups that produced them.

Inspect the evidence

Compare observed cohort failures, task mix, drift, and versions with held-out evaluation.

Decision boundary / trap

Production regression starts an investigation or rollback, not automatic retraining.

LoRA / adapter release

An adapter release depends on its compatible base, evaluated artifact, serving integration, and actual request route. Start from live behavior and verify each identity.

Compatible baseSituation

The adapter cannot be used with the chosen base model or runtime, even though the model family name looks similar.

What this means

Model selection means choosing a supported model that meets the actual task, quality, modality, latency, and cost requirements.

Inspect the evidence

Identify the exact supported base model/revision, tokenizer, and serving runtime.

Decision boundary / trap

A same-family model name does not prove adapter compatibility.

Task examplesSituation

The adapter learns the wrong task boundaries or fails a specialised cohort absent from its examples.

What this means

Dataset splits separate training examples, tuning/validation examples, and independent final tests. Lineage records where each version came from.

Inspect the evidence

Check the versioned examples and held-out cohorts used to train and evaluate this adapter.

Decision boundary / trap

Small adapter artifacts do not reduce the need for good supervision.

LoRA configurationSituation

Increasing rank makes the adapter larger or more expensive, but held-out quality stays flat or gets worse.

What this means

LoRA rank controls the capacity of the small trainable adapter. Scaling and dropout also affect its training behavior.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect rank/scaling/dropout and training settings against validation results.

Decision boundary / trap

Higher rank is not a cure for wrong labels or leakage.

Adapter trainingSituation

The tuning job fails or produces an unexpected artifact; the assumed adapter-only training setup was not actually applied.

What this means

LoRA learns small adapter weights while the base model stays frozen. The adapter modifies that compatible base model’s behavior.

Inspect the evidence

Confirm the intended base remained frozen and the expected adapter artifact was produced.

Decision boundary / trap

LoRA changes adapter weights; it is not retrieval or a standalone model.

Artifact / base pairingSituation

Loading fails, or the adapter produces poor output when paired with a different base revision, tokenizer, or prompt format.

What this means

An unmerged LoRA adapter must be paired with the compatible base revision, tokenizer/template, and supported artifact format.

Inspect the evidence

Check adapter/base versions, tokenizer/template, artifact format, and merged versus unmerged status.

Decision boundary / trap

An unmerged adapter needs its compatible base at inference.

Release gateSituation

The adapter passes one evaluation configuration but fails when combined with the actual base, template, or serving settings.

What this means

Held-out evaluation tests a candidate on representative examples it was not trained or tuned to memorize.

Inspect the evidence

Evaluate the actual base+adapter pair with the intended inference configuration and cohorts.

Decision boundary / trap

Evaluating a different base or template invalidates the release comparison.

Version / approvalSituation

The new adapter is marked approved, yet users still receive the previous adapter’s behaviour because approval did not load it.

What this means

Artifact registration and approval record which version may be released. They do not perform the live deployment.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect registered artifact, approval, lineage, and rollback pair.

Decision boundary / trap

Registry approval does not load or hot-swap the live adapter.

Load / route adapterSituation

Requests behave like the unadapted base model or the wrong task adapter, despite a valid adapter artifact existing.

What this means

Adapter serving loads the intended base and adapter and routes each authorized request to the right pair.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect deployed base/component, adapter readiness, actual selected identity, and tenant entitlement.

Decision boundary / trap

Use the supported adapter-serving contract; generic model registration is insufficient.

Live smoke / rollbackSituation

A live smoke request does not match the approved base/adapter pair, or rollback restores only part of the previous configuration.

What this means

Live verification checks which model, adapter, prompt, and route actually serve a real application request.

Inspect the evidence

Compare attributed live requests with the approved pair; verify rollback restores the pair and route.

Decision boundary / trap

Base-like output can be a loading/routing defect, not failed training.

Live adapter behaviorSituation

One adapter or tenant route degrades while overall endpoint health and average latency still look normal.

What this means

Production monitoring connects real task outcomes and failures to the versions and user groups that produced them.

Inspect the evidence

Correlate outcomes with adapter/base versions, task cohorts, loading failures, and request scope.

Decision boundary / trap

Aggregate endpoint metrics can hide one broken adapter or tenant route.

Inference / latency / cost

Separate queue wait, initialization, model generation, transport buffering, and repeated work before choosing a performance capability.

Task / model fitSituation

The application meets latency or price targets but fails the task, or a more expensive model adds no measured useful quality.

What this means

Model selection means choosing a supported model that meets the actual task, quality, modality, latency, and cost requirements.

Inspect the evidence

Compare measured quality, token use, latency, and cost across suitable supported models.

Decision boundary / trap

A smaller/faster model must still meet the task quality target.

Representation / runtimeSituation

The reduced-precision model fits memory but loses important task quality or shows no speed improvement on the target runtime.

What this means

Quantization reduces the precision used to represent model weights. Its memory, speed, and quality effects depend on the serving setup.

Inspect the evidence

Benchmark supported precision and serving settings with the actual hardware/runtime and quality gates.

Decision boundary / trap

Lower precision does not guarantee lower end-to-end latency.

Serving identitySituation

The endpoint responds, but its output or timing differs from the intended model/container/configuration tested before release.

What this means

Live verification checks which model, adapter, prompt, and route actually serve a real application request.

Inspect the evidence

Verify the intended model/container/component/configuration is ready and receiving requests.

Decision boundary / trap

An endpoint being reachable does not identify the release it serves.

Capacity / routingSituation

Requests throttle or slow under load because demand exceeds available quota/capacity, or routing reaches an unapproved destination.

What this means

Capacity is the amount of inference work the configured service or endpoint can handle under its quotas and routing rules.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect demand, quotas, utilization, scaling, approved destinations, and selected capacity mode.

Decision boundary / trap

Cross-Region routing, reserved capacity, and application failover are different controls.

Admission / queue waitSituation

Users see 429 errors or long waits during bursts; accepted work accumulates faster than model capacity can process it.

What this means

Admission controls which requests enter; queueing and worker pacing determine when accepted work reaches the model.

Inspect the evidence

Measure accepted token demand, throttles, queue age, worker pacing, and tenant budgets.

Decision boundary / trap

Concurrency limits do not express every token-rate requirement.

Repeated workSituation

Equivalent permitted work is repeated unnecessarily, or an incorrectly scoped cache returns stale or another tenant’s results.

What this means

Caching reuses a specific kind of compatible work: an answer, an embedding, or a supported prompt prefix.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect exact scoped result reuse, compatible embedding reuse, or supported prompt-prefix hits.

Decision boundary / trap

Prompt caching does not reuse the complete answer.

Generation workSituation

Answers generate far more tokens than needed, making total latency and cost high even when the first token arrives quickly.

What this means

Generation settings control limits and behavior such as output length, stop sequences, and sampling. They do not establish factual truth.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect context/output token counts, stop limits, and actual generation configuration.

Decision boundary / trap

Longer output can dominate total latency even when the first token is fast.

Stage timingsSituation

The first token is fast but completion is slow, or total request time is high without evidence identifying which stage consumed it.

What this means

Stage timings measure where time was spent across queueing, initialization, retrieval, generation, and delivery.

Inspect the evidence

Separate queue, initialization, retrieval, model first-token/generation, and transport spans.

Decision boundary / trap

Optimize the measured bottleneck; an uninstrumented hop is not proven fast.

Delivery contractSituation

The model emits tokens incrementally, but the browser receives one late response because a transport hop buffers them.

What this means

The delivered result must satisfy the user’s request and be checked against evidence or the authoritative business outcome.

Inspect the evidence

Check synchronous/streaming/background mode and buffering at every transport hop.

Decision boundary / trap

Streaming improves early delivery while the caller waits; it is not asynchronous completion.

User outcome / costSituation

A cheap or fast invocation produces so many failed tasks or retries that users experience poor outcomes and higher total cost.

What this means

Performance should be judged by usable outcomes: latency experienced by users, successful tasks, and the cost of producing them.

Inspect the evidence

Compare p95/first-token/total latency and cost per successful task across cohorts.

Decision boundary / trap

Low invocation cost can hide retries, failures, or poor task quality.

Agent / durable workflow / tools

Start from the authoritative business outcome. Trace validation, tool calls, state, retries, and the authority that chose each step.

Caller / requirementSituation

The system accepts a request without verified scope, or returns a live success message for work that is still only queued.

What this means

The entry point establishes the caller, their permitted request, and whether they expect a live response or a durable background job.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect trusted caller scope, requested business outcome, and job/delivery contract.

Decision boundary / trap

A natural-language request does not establish write authority.

Who chooses next?Situation

A fixed approval process uses unpredictable model-selected actions, or a tool-selection task is forced into an unsuitable rigid sequence.

What this means

Orchestration determines who controls the next action: explicit workflow states, model-selected tools, or event-driven workers.

Inspect the evidence

Check whether transitions are known states, model-selected tools, or independently delivered events.

Decision boundary / trap

Complexity alone does not justify an agent.

Durable state / waitsSituation

A long approval wait loses progress, retries restart completed work, or a callback resumes the wrong execution.

What this means

A durable workflow records progress through known steps, retries, timeouts, and approval waits.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect applicable workflow history, state, retries, timeout, callback identity, and approval.

Decision boundary / trap

A model-generated plan is not durable execution state.

Tool choiceSituation

The agent chooses an unsuitable tool, repeatedly loops, or attempts an action beyond the caller’s permitted scope.

What this means

An agent chooses tools using the task and observations, within the allowed actions and execution limits.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect observations, allowed tools, chosen action, iteration/token limits, and scoped authority.

Decision boundary / trap

An agent framework does not grant permission or ensure correct business choices.

Arguments / preconditionsSituation

The tool arguments are valid JSON, but the refund amount, account, permission, or transaction precondition is invalid.

What this means

Tool validation checks arguments, caller permission, and business preconditions before an external action is allowed.

Inspect the evidence

Check parameter schema, tenant/business authorization, transaction rules, and required approval.

Decision boundary / trap

Valid JSON is not a valid or authorized transaction.

Tool executionSituation

A tool times out or reports an error, but it is unclear whether the external business operation already completed.

What this means

Tool execution is the actual API or business operation. A returned error and the business record must be checked separately.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect tool logs, dependencies, runtime limits, errors, and the authoritative returned result.

Decision boundary / trap

A tool timeout does not prove its side effect failed.

Recovery / duplicatesSituation

A retry or duplicate message creates a second payment, ticket, or other write for the same original request.

What this means

Recovery reconciles uncertain results and retries. Idempotency prevents repeated delivery from repeating the same business action.

Inspect the evidence

Check durable work identity, retries, DLQ, idempotency, and outcome reconciliation.

Decision boundary / trap

Repeated delivery must not cause a duplicate business write.

Business outcomeSituation

The agent says the action succeeded, but the authoritative business record is unchanged or the durable job remains incomplete.

What this means

The delivered result must satisfy the user’s request and be checked against evidence or the authoritative business outcome.

Inspect the evidence

Compare the claimed completion with the authoritative record and persisted job status.

Decision boundary / trap

A fluent answer or accepted job is not completed work.

Access / safety / sensitive copies

Identify the actual exposure boundary. Authorization, safety filtering, private transport, encryption, and retention protect different things.

Trusted identitySituation

The caller is unauthenticated, the effective identity differs from expectations, or an applicable policy denies the attempted AWS action.

What this means

Authentication establishes who is calling. Effective roles and policies determine their allowed AWS actions.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect authentication context, effective roles/policies, and caller attribution.

Decision boundary / trap

Identity proves who called, not which tenant documents they may retrieve.

Data / tool scopeSituation

Tenant A receives tenant B’s passage or can request an action against a record it does not own.

What this means

Data and tool scope restrict the caller to the documents, records, and actions they are entitled to use.

Inspect the evidence

Verify caller-to-resource entitlement, fail-closed metadata filters, and bypass paths before context or writes.

Decision boundary / trap

Guardrails cannot replace tenant authorization.

Network pathSituation

An application in private subnets still invokes the public service endpoint, or a direct route bypasses the intended endpoint policy.

What this means

A private network path uses the intended endpoint, DNS, routing, and policies rather than an unintended public route.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect actual DNS/endpoint/routing/policies and direct public bypass routes.

Decision boundary / trap

Private transport does not itself establish resource entitlement or allowed residency.

Encrypted copiesSituation

A required derived copy is unencrypted, or a supposedly authorised service cannot read it because key access is missing.

What this means

Encryption protects stored and transmitted copies; key policies determine who can use the encryption keys.

Inspect the evidence

Check source, index, intermediate, job, and log encryption plus effective key access.

Decision boundary / trap

Encryption does not sanitize content or authorize a tenant.

Content / injectionSituation

A harmful response or injected document/tool instruction reaches the model or an external action without the required checks.

What this means

Content safety checks address harmful content and untrusted instructions. They are separate from document or transaction authorization.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect untrusted document/tool inputs, applied safety checks, and deterministic output/business validation.

Decision boundary / trap

A content filter is not a transaction authorization boundary.

PII transformationSituation

Sensitive names or identifiers remain in an index, request, or result even though a detection job reported finding them.

What this means

PII handling detects sensitive personal information and applies the required verified masking, redaction, or retention rules.

Inspect the evidence

Check where sensitive spans exist and verify required masking/redaction actually happened.

Decision boundary / trap

Detection is not verified redaction.

Retention / destinationsSituation

Deleted source content remains in caches or indexes, retained copies outlive policy, or processing occurs in an unapproved location.

What this means

Governance controls permitted processing locations, permission ceilings, retention, and deletion across original and derived copies.

Inspect the evidence

Inventory source and derived copies, processing destinations, retention, deletion, and applicable policy ceilings.

Decision boundary / trap

Private encryption or not-used-for-training is not a complete residency/retention guarantee.

Observed exposureSituation

The displayed answer masks personal information, but invocation logs, tool logs, or cached results still retain the original sensitive input.

What this means

Exposure includes what reached users, tools, caches, and retained logs—not only the final answer shown on screen.

Inspect the evidence

Inspect safely scoped evidence of what reached users, tools, caches, and logs, with request/version identity.

Decision boundary / trap

Filtered output can coexist with sensitive pre-filter logs; protect every retained copy.

Decision boundary / Trap

Map explanations are available below when interaction is unavailable.

Requirements

Define the business problem and the outcome the application must produce before selecting a model. Is the task summarization, classification, reasoning over supplied evidence, or proposing a tool action? Establish why a GenAI component fits, and keep exact business rules and action authority in deterministic controls.

  • What does success mean? Define the expected answer or action, difficult examples, and critical cohorts—not just fluent output.
  • What must the model work with? Identify input modalities, context size, and whether facts are supplied, private, or frequently changing.
  • What limits the solution? Record quality, safety, latency, cost, approved data locations, access scope, and any required approval.

Decision to make: Turn these requirements into representative held-out cases. Select then compares model/task fit. Clearer instructions or examples address task/format gaps; RAG supplies required evidence; supported customization is a candidate when stable behavior still fails evaluated prompting. Compare measured benefit and lifecycle cost rather than assuming a larger model is necessary.

Capabilities: Representative evaluation cases first; then suitable model inference, prompt/context, retrieval, or supported customization.

Decision boundary / trap: Model size and public benchmark rank do not prove workload fit. Identify whether the gap is task definition, evidence, model capability, or stable behavior before changing weights.

The team assumes it needs the largest model

Situation: A team needs concise summaries and reliable categories within a strict latency and token-cost budget. It proposes the largest available model before testing representative inputs.

What this means: The requirement is measured task quality under constraints. Model size is a candidate characteristic, not an acceptance criterion.

Inspect the evidence: Compare supported candidates on the same held-out cases, including difficult inputs and critical cohorts. Check capability, context/output limits, quality, latency, and cost.

Decision boundary / trap: Choose by representative workload fit; public benchmark rank or model size alone is insufficient.

Answers need current private facts

Situation: An assistant explains policies clearly but cannot answer questions about recently changed internal rules. The team proposes fine-tuning to make every future answer current.

What this means: The missing requirement is access to fresh, permitted evidence. Changing weights alone does not supply a live authoritative source.

Inspect the evidence: Check source freshness, caller entitlement, whether the required fact reaches context, and whether citations support the answer.

Decision boundary / trap: Private/current/attributable knowledge → evaluate RAG. RAG and customization can combine when their requirements differ.

Format and task rules are unclear

Situation: Equivalent inputs receive different categories and inconsistent output shapes. The team has not defined category boundaries, supplied examples, or validated the business meaning of the result.

What this means: Clarify what a correct answer means before treating the behavior as a model-capability or training defect.

Inspect the evidence: Review task definitions, governing instructions, representative examples, supported output constraints, and schema plus business assertions.

Decision boundary / trap: Task/format gaps → start with prompting and supported structured output. Valid JSON or low temperature is not proof of a correct decision.

Stable behavior still fails clear prompts

Situation: The team has clear task rules, correct evidence, and evaluated prompt examples. A suitable baseline still misses a required stable style or classification behavior across representative cases.

What this means: Supported customization may fit an evaluated behavior gap. This differs from missing current evidence or ambiguous instructions.

Inspect the evidence: Check supervision quality, held-out improvement, safety/cohort regressions, lifecycle cost, and compatibility with the intended deployment.

Decision boundary / trap: Consider supported customization only for the measured gap; evaluate it against prompting/RAG baselines and verify deployment support.

Fluent output hides an invalid business action

Situation: An assistant proposes a well-formed refund request for an account outside the caller’s scope. The team proposes a larger model instead of enforcing the business preconditions.

What this means: Language quality does not establish authorization or valid transaction semantics. Identify the control requirement independently of model choice.

Inspect the evidence: Inspect the effective caller, permitted record/action scope, actual tool arguments, approval requirements, and authoritative business outcome.

Decision boundary / trap: Enforce deterministic authorization and action checks. A fluent answer or valid JSON is not a completed, permitted business action.

Data

Version approved training/tuning data and separate representative held-out evaluation data with source/tool references.

Decision boundary / trap: Tuning on the held-out final test invalidates its independence.

Select

Compare supported model capability, modalities, context limits, quality, safety, latency, cost, and deployment requirements.

Decision boundary / trap: A public benchmark rank does not establish fit for this workload.

Customize / train

Change the model only for an evaluated need. Fine-tuning uses suitable labeled data; continued pre-training uses suitable unlabeled domain text where supported; distillation trains an eligible smaller student from teacher-generated behavior. LoRA is a fine-tuning technique, not a separate source of knowledge. An unchanged selected model can proceed to evaluation.

Capabilities: Eligible Bedrock model customization or SageMaker training according to support/control needs.

Decision boundary / trap: RAG is not fine-tuning and neither is required for every model change.

Fine-tune

Use suitable labeled training data for an evaluated stable behavior/task need when supported prompting is insufficient.

Capabilities: Eligible Bedrock model customization or SageMaker training according to support/control needs.

Decision boundary / trap: Daily private-document refresh and citations are not implemented merely by changing weights.

Pre-train

Adapt eligible models on suitable unlabeled domain text where the model/feature supports it; evaluate against the original baseline.

Capabilities: Supported continued pre-training or an appropriate controlled training workflow.

Decision boundary / trap: This option is model-specific and not a real-time source lookup.

Domain adaptation is mistaken for live knowledge

Situation: A domain-adapted model still gives an outdated policy after the original document changes. The team assumes continued pre-training should remove the need to retrieve current evidence.

What this means: Domain adaptation changes eligible model behavior using suitable text; it is not a real-time source lookup.

Inspect the evidence: Compare the source/version and context supplied for this request. Evaluate the adapted model against the original baseline on representative held-out tasks.

Decision boundary / trap: Continued pre-training is model-specific and does not replace current evidence retrieval.

Distill

Train an eligible smaller student from teacher-generated behavior using a supported workflow and representative tasks. Compare held-out quality, latency, and cost.

Capabilities: Eligible Bedrock distillation or a controlled SageMaker training workflow.

Decision boundary / trap: Distillation is different from quantizing the same model or attaching a LoRA adapter.

The cheaper student loses a critical task

Situation: A smaller distilled student reduces serving cost but fails a critical cohort that the teacher handled correctly. Average quality remains acceptable.

What this means: Lower cost is useful only when the student preserves the required task quality, including critical cohorts.

Inspect the evidence: Compare teacher/student outputs on the same held-out tasks; inspect cohort quality, safety, latency, and cost before promotion.

Decision boundary / trap: Do not promote an average improvement that violates a critical requirement. Distillation differs from quantization or adding an adapter.

Evaluate + approve

Measure quality, correctness, faithfulness, safety, latency, and cost; use calibrated automated/judge checks and accountable human review where needed.

Capabilities: Supported Bedrock evaluations, deterministic checks, expert review, and approval workflows.

Decision boundary / trap: Human review and automated evaluation complement each other; neither is automatically infallible.

Deploy

Release a compatible approved model/prompt/retrieval configuration with version attribution and rollback.

Decision boundary / trap: A registered artifact does not automatically update an endpoint.

Monitor

Correlate production versions and outcomes, turn failures into regressions, and roll back critical degradation.

Decision boundary / trap: A monitoring chart does not itself generate calibrated quality scores.

Source

Approved facts, media, and datasets enter here. Establish provenance, versions, permitted use, and update/delete behavior before creating derived copies.

Capabilities: Amazon S3, supported database/connectors, and authoritative business APIs.

Decision boundary / trap: Changing a source object does not prove the index, cache, or generated answer was refreshed.

Preprocess

Convert or validate inputs before creating chunks, embeddings, datasets, or model requests. Preserve meaning rather than merely producing text.

Capabilities: Textract, Transcribe, Glue/Data Quality, Comprehend, or supported Bedrock Data Automation.

Decision boundary / trap: Detection is not redaction, and accurate embeddings cannot restore missing extracted text.

Ingestion

Build searchable evidence: Parse → Chunk → Metadata → Embed → Index. This is preparation/synchronization work, not the per-question ranking path.

Capabilities: Bedrock Knowledge Bases ingestion with supported parsers, chunking, embedding model, and vector store.

Decision boundary / trap: A Lambda ingestion transformation does not control query-time ranking.

Knowledge store

Keep searchable chunks, vectors, metadata, and source references. A Knowledge Base coordinates RAG; its vector store holds/searches the indexed evidence.

Capabilities: Bedrock Knowledge Bases with OpenSearch or another supported vector store.

Decision boundary / trap: OpenSearch does not automatically mean custom RAG. A vector database is not an enterprise assistant.

User / API

Accept a request with trusted identity, its task, and an appropriate delivery contract. Carry scope and correlation through downstream stages.

Capabilities: API Gateway + application adapter/router; Cognito or federation where appropriate.

Decision boundary / trap: Authentication identifies the caller; it does not establish document or tool entitlement.

Retrieval

Turn a question into permitted candidates, rank them, and select evidence for context. Query → query embedding → vector/lexical/hybrid → candidates → reranker → best context.

Capabilities: Knowledge Bases, supported OpenSearch lexical/vector/hybrid search, and supported Bedrock reranking.

Decision boundary / trap: Reranking cannot recover material absent from its candidate input.

Prompt / context

System instructions + prompt template + user query + retrieved knowledge + conversation context become the model input. Keep untrusted data separate from governing instructions.

Capabilities: Prompt Management; Converse/ConverseStream or model-specific APIs with application-managed context.

Decision boundary / trap: A versioned prompt, valid JSON, or low temperature does not establish factual truth.

Model

Invoke a compatible evaluated model using permitted context. Choose the hosting boundary by required controls, not by whether something is “custom.”

Capabilities: Amazon Bedrock for managed FM-centric integration; SageMaker AI when deeper ML/hosting control is decisive.

Decision boundary / trap: Custom does not automatically mean SageMaker. Bedrock also supports eligible customization.

Response

Deliver and validate the result under the caller’s contract. An answer, source citation, tool outcome, and durable job completion are different artifacts.

Capabilities: Converse / ConverseStream; asynchronous jobs/workers; supported Bedrock batch inference.

Decision boundary / trap: Streaming is not asynchronous. A job acknowledgment is not completed business work.

Orchestration

Choose who controls progress across either data or runtime work: bounded code, explicit states, decoupled events, or model-selected actions.

Capabilities: Lambda | Step Functions | EventBridge / SQS | Bedrock Agents or an appropriate agent framework.

Decision boundary / trap: An agent framework does not replace durable workflow state or business authorization.

Security / governance

Apply identity, access, isolation, encryption, network, safety, PII, and governance controls at the boundaries they protect—not as one final filter.

Capabilities: Authentication + IAM/data authorization + isolation + KMS + network policy + appropriate safety/PII controls.

Decision boundary / trap: Guardrails is not authorization. Private transport or encryption does not establish entitlement or approved residency.

Evaluation

Measure evidence coverage, answer/task quality, safety, latency, and cost before releases and during operation. Diagnose backwards using observed boundary evidence.

Capabilities: Recall/precision, faithfulness/correctness/relevance, safety, task success, first-token/total latency, and cost per successful outcome.

Decision boundary / trap: High average quality, a real citation, or low latency can hide a critical cohort or unsafe side effect.

Observability

Collect the evidence needed for the question: trends, caller activity, interaction content, or time across request stages.

Capabilities: CloudWatch | CloudTrail | Bedrock Model Invocation Logging | X-Ray / OpenTelemetry | agent/tool traces.

Decision boundary / trap: Enabling Lambda tracing does not expose every uninstrumented SDK hop or hidden model internal.

1. Read the constraint before choosing the service

For every scenario, complete this reasoning chain:

  1. Hard constraint: what must hold? Consider identity, data location, duration, approval, latency, recovery, and delivery mode.
  2. Pattern: bounded request, durable workflow, queue, event routing, agent, retrieval, stream, or batch?
  3. Ownership: does a managed capability fit? If not, is there a supported extension? Own only the layer that still needs custom behavior, then choose its AWS services.
  4. Controls: where do authorization, safety, encryption, audit, retention, and recovery apply?
  5. Runner-up: which requirement does the nearest alternative violate? What change would make it appropriate?

“Least operational overhead,” “most cost-effective,” and “lowest latency” are tiebreakers after hard requirements are met. Separate first visible token, total response time, queue delay, and retrieval latency. Cost includes idle capacity, tokens, storage, transfer, and operations.

Architecture framework: the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens applies GenAI guidance across all six Well-Architected pillars and the model/application lifecycle. It extends the framework; model selection, RAG, and responsible AI are topics within it, not replacement pillars. Use it to review a PoC and production design against measured quality, latency, cost, and business goals. Generative AI Lens.

2. Learn the exam traps by domain

Use the domain recap for quick recall, then test the boundary in a scenario. The practice questions are original, single-answer exercises; the real exam also includes multiple-response questions.

Domain trap recap

Recall the decision, then check the tempting substitute. Open one domain at a time; detailed concepts stay in the mindmap.

Domain 1 · 31% · Model, data, and prompt decisionsChoose from representative evidence; customize only the responsibility that needs it.
Select on your workload

Compare supported models using representative held-out inputs, capability/modality, limits, safety, latency, cost, and Region/API support.

Trap: Public benchmark rank alone is insufficient.

Prompt, RAG, or customization?

Format/examples/tone → prompting and supported structured output. Private/current/attributable knowledge → RAG. Stable behavior still fails evaluated prompts → supported customization.

Trap: Validate schema AND business meaning. Low temperature is not truth or determinism. RAG and customization can combine; assess data quality, benefit, lifecycle cost, and serving support.

Managed RAG or custom layer?

Use Knowledge Bases with a supported store; use a supported Lambda transformation for custom chunking. Own query orchestration or retrieval only where the managed contract does not fit.

Trap: OpenSearch does not automatically mean custom RAG. Custom chunking alone does not force rebuilding ingestion, retrieval, and citations. Extra control adds operations cost.

Search and context boundaries

Semantic intent → vector retrieval. Exact IDs → exact lookup, lexical, or supported hybrid. Lost passage context → evaluate chunking/overlap or parent-child retrieval.

Trap: Preserve searchable identifiers and measure recall. Hybrid is not universally superior. Evaluate chunking/overlap or parent-child retrieval; larger chunks dilute precision/use tokens, semantic chunking is not a universal default, and GraphRAG has a different contract.

Data preparation must be a gate

Validate extracted structure before database/index writes. Apply and verify required PII redaction; use explicit Glue/Data Quality failure or quarantine rules for invalid records.

Trap: A report is not a gate; IsComplete alone does not validate non-empty text. Preserve layout and speaker turns, but do not treat speaker labels as verified roles. Fix detached PDF columns before chunking; check native audio support before requiring text conversion.

Versioned configuration is not a release gate

Prompt Management versions reusable instructions. AppConfig deployment + polling/extension changes application routing. Model/LoRA releases need evaluation → governed artifact/approval → compatible serving/deployment.

Trap: Versions do not prove quality or approval. AppConfig is not instantaneous global mutation. Registry alone does not update endpoints or hot-swap adapters.

Changed/deleted source still appears

Check completed synchronization, ingestion failures, update/delete handling, and derived copies; coalesce/pace StartIngestionJob requests.

Trap: An S3 update alone does not prove index refresh. Check freshness, entitlement, recall, context budget, and citation support.

Domain 2 · 26% · Execution, integration, and recoveryChoose who controls progress before choosing the runner.
Task, workflow, or agent?

One bounded stateless operation → Lambda. Known durable states/retries/approval → Step Functions. Model-selected next tools → bounded agent. Long-lived/custom runtime → suitable ECS/Fargate or agent hosting.

Trap: Externalize durable state; conventional Lambda invocations are limited to 15 minutes. Persistent processes differ from session state; GPU/host needs require suitable hosting. Complexity alone does not justify orchestration. AgentCore Runtime hosts agents; the implementation or managed harness owns the loop.

Dynamic diagnosis, controlled write

Agent proposes → validate scope/parameters → durable approval/action workflow where required.

Trap: The business API still enforces authorization, approval, and idempotency. Bound tool scope, iterations, time, and tokens; a framework does not supply business authorization.

Buffering or routing?

SQS → absorb bursts and pace workers. EventBridge → route events to independent targets; add queues where buffering is needed.

Trap: Queue age, visibility timeout, DLQ, retries, and rate control matter. Shared workers distribute work rather than broadcast it to every consumer. Concurrency alone is not a model token-rate limit.

S3 event starts a workflow

S3 EventBridge delivery → rule → Step Functions. For object bursts, filter keys, buffer, then pace.

Trap: Direct bucket notifications cannot target a state machine or SQS FIFO.

Prompt chain or conversation API?

Bedrock Flows → supported typed nodes/branches. Converse/ConverseStream → common supported-model chat API. Keep authoritative state, validate intent/entities, and request missing fields.

Trap: Flows is not model-selected next-action reasoning. The application supplies relevant message history; an inference call is not a conversation store. InvokeModel can also implement chat with a model-specific contract.

Acknowledgement or delivery?

Immediate acknowledgement → valid proxy response/direct integration plus tracked job state. WebSocket tokens → decode stream events and send to the connection ID.

Trap: Async acceptance is not business completion. Storing a connection ID does not resume a model stream.

Shared implementation standards

Use application/Lambda code for lightweight normalization/schema checks; versioned infrastructure constructs + runtime wrappers + CI for consistent redaction/logging. Q Developer can assist IDE review/edit/test.

Trap: Preserve meaningful identifiers/case; Comprehend is not arbitrary query normalization. Review the actual diff and execute tests; avoid obsolete command syntax.

Domain 3 · 20% · Security, governance, and evidenceIdentity, access, safety, privacy, and residency are separate controls.
Identity is not entitlement

Cognito/federation authenticates callers; IAM + application/data authorization limits actions and business data. Roles Anywhere uses trusted CA/X.509 credentials for eligible headless workloads.

Trap: Authentication and directory integration alone do not establish document/tool permission. Authorize backend scope → ACL/filter → retrieval; the ingestion role does not authorize every caller to every vector.

Guardrails is not authorization

Use supported Guardrails input/output policies and deterministic checks for content risks; enforce tool/data permission separately.

Trap: Schema compliance is not factual correctness. Retrieved documents/tool results can carry injection; safety filtering does not enforce tenant access. Lake Formation filters do not block independent direct S3 access.

Find PII, then verify transformation

S3 discovery → Macie; text pipeline → Comprehend; model I/O → Guardrails.

Trap: Detection is not verified redaction, and filtered output does not sanitize all logs or derived copies.

Private path and encryption

Interface VPC endpoint/PrivateLink + private DNS + network/endpoint policy/IAM → private role-restricted inference. KMS/TLS/Secrets Manager + least privilege → bytes and secrets.

Trap: A private subnet alone does not create the private service path. Remove bypasses. Encryption does not establish entitlement, residency, or deletion.

Permission ceilings and findings

SCPs/permissions boundaries limit applicable permissions. Config checks supported resource configuration; GuardDuty detects supported threats; Security Hub aggregates supported findings.

Trap: Ceilings do not grant access; explicit denies still apply. Config does not inspect every prompt; threat/finding services are not inline content filters or detectors of every GenAI attack.

Which evidence answers the audit question?

AWS API caller/time/location → CloudTrail with required event coverage. Prompt/response → explicitly enabled, protected Bedrock invocation logging for supported calls.

Trap: API metadata is not prompt content. Logs can contain sensitive input, including pre-masking input; apply access, encryption, retention, and delivery monitoring.

One Region, geography, or global?

Exactly one approved Region → in-Region inference. Approved geographic destinations → eligible geographic profile. No geographic restriction → evaluate eligible global/geographic profiles.

Trap: Check EVERY destination: geography labels are insufficient for a permitted subset. Private encrypted transport does not authorize another Region. Source-Region application recovery and retention/deletion of all derived copies remain separate.

Domain 4 · 12% · Cost, latency, and operational efficiencyIdentify the repeated work and measure the actual bottleneck.
Intermittent or stable throughput?

Flexible intermittent traffic → on-demand. Stable measured token demand → evaluate Provisioned Throughput.

Trap: On-demand still has quotas/throttles. Check hourly billing, sizing, support, and commitment; no universal 60–70% break-even or guaranteed lower p99.

Offline completion or earlier tokens?

Supported offline S3 dataset → Bedrock batch inference. Earlier visible output while waiting → streaming with end-to-end transport.

Trap: Check job semantics, record reconciliation, model/Region support, and completion objectives. Streaming is not async and need not make generation faster/cheaper; handle buffering, disconnects, and partial failures. Avoid universal batch discount/latency claims.

Capacity pool or model routing?

Cross-Region profile → broader eligible compute pool. Intelligent Prompt Routing or custom routing/cascade → simpler queries use less capability.

Trap: Geographic controls/source-endpoint recovery remain separate. Evaluate both query groups; native routing has model-pair/family restrictions. Custom routing does not inherently need Step Functions.

Prefix cache or answer cache?

Identical long prefix/questions differ → Bedrock prompt caching. Equivalent questions/valid answer → semantic response cache. Identical complete scoped input/configuration → exact cache/fingerprint.

Trap: Prompt cache hits still generate; check supported checkpoints, TTL, hits, and billing. Answer caches can skip generation only with a valid entry. Calibrate similarity, scope, freshness, expiry/eviction/invalidation, and unsafe reuse.

Metrics, spans, or log queries?

Changing latency/tokens/throttles/errors/queue age → CloudWatch metrics/alarms. Slow/failed hop → instrumented X-Ray/OTel spans. Across-call prompt/version patterns → Logs Insights over configured logs.

Trap: Custom quality signals need evaluation/instrumentation. Lambda tracing alone does not expose every SDK call or hidden model stage.

Domain 5 · 11% · Evaluation, diagnosis, and release decisionsFind the first failed boundary; test outcomes before promotion.
Evidence missing or poorly ordered?

Missing → inspect ingestion, freshness, source versions, ACLs/filters, query/chunking, and recall. Present but poorly ordered → rerank. Noisy context → evaluate precision, ranking, chunk boundaries, and pruning.

Trap: Reranking reorders existing candidates and adds latency/cost. Neither reranking nor a larger generator recovers unseen evidence; preserve relevant evidence when pruning.

Faithfulness, relevance, or task completion?

Invented claims → source faithfulness. Off-question answer → answer relevance/task rubric. Fluent wrong action → actual tool selection/parameters, authorization, idempotency, and completion.

Trap: Citation presence is not source support. Correctness, relevance, and faithfulness differ. Use source-fact/business assertions plus factuality evaluation before promotion.

Trace, judge, expert, or assertion?

Agent failure → correlated agent trace + tool logs/workflow history. Semantic assessment at scale → calibrated LLM judge. High-risk labels → experts with guidelines/adjudication. Repeatable regressions → assertions/suitable automated metrics.

Trap: Persist required trace events; memory summaries are different evidence. Judges need rubrics and human calibration/bias checks; humans are fallible. BLEU/ROUGE overlap is not semantic truth or tool correctness.

Compare before or during exposure?

Offline → same held-out cases/sources/rubric. A/B → live outcome comparison with stable cohorts and attribution.

Trap: Apply prior safety gates and gather enough evidence; no mandatory 50/50 split. Block a release that improves averages but breaks a critical cohort or repeats a business write.

Canary, shadow, blue/green, or probe?

Canary → small live cohort + stop/rollback + gradual promotion. Shadow → mirrored requests without candidate responses. Blue/green → switch prepared environments. Synthetic canary → scheduled integration probe.

Trap: Isolate shadow side effects and account for duplicated data/cost. Validate rollback/state compatibility. Uptime alone does not prove factual quality.

DOMAIN STUDY + INTERACTIVE PRACTICE Learn the trap. Choose the right AWS service.

Pick a domain → try a multiple-choice question → learn the service distinction.

These are original practice questions. Open a question, choose A–D yourself, then reveal the solution. “Learn the distinction” remains available without JavaScript.

Domain 1 · 31% · Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance

Choose models, knowledge architectures, retrieval, chunking, and prompt governance.

RAG vs. fine-tuning vs. prompting

PDF trap 1 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • Bedrock model customization
  • Bedrock Prompt Management
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A manufacturer runs a support assistant on Amazon Bedrock. Its private product manuals are stored in Amazon S3 and updated every day. Answers must reflect the latest approved manual and identify the source passage. The team wants to minimize ongoing model-training work. The application already follows the requested response style, but previously correct answers become stale after source updates. A prompt-only prototype cannot access the private manuals. The source set fits the supported managed ingestion path. Which solution best meets these requirements?

  1. Synchronize approved S3 documents into Bedrock Knowledge Bases and retrieve source passages for each generated answer.
  2. Fine-tune a supported Bedrock model on each approved manual update and rely on the customized model for source facts.
  3. Version the system prompt in Prompt Management with manual summaries and retain the existing prompt-only request path.
  4. Store generated answers in a question-keyed cache and extend cache lifetime to reduce calls after document updates.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

Daily document updates and source attribution require current evidence at inference time.

Why this answer fits

A. Synchronize approved S3 documents into Bedrock Knowledge Bases and retrieve source passages for each generated answer.

Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to index the approved manuals and retrieve relevant passages for each question. Retrieval supplies the changing facts and source references without retraining model weights for every update. Keep ingestion synchronized so the retrieved evidence actually reflects the latest approved manual.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Fine-tune a supported Bedrock model on each approved manual update and rely on the customized model for source facts.

    Daily fine-tuning adds the training work the team wants to avoid and does not itself provide passage-level evidence for each answer.

  2. Version the system prompt in Prompt Management with manual summaries and retain the existing prompt-only request path.

    Manual titles and instructions do not supply the private passages needed to answer or cite the question.

  3. Store generated answers in a question-keyed cache and extend cache lifetime to reduce calls after document updates.

    Reusing answers after a manual update can return outdated facts; a cache is not the source-refresh mechanism.

What would change the answer?

If the evidence is already supplied and the remaining problem is consistent terminology or response style, test prompt changes and then consider supported fine-tuning.

How the services fit together
  1. Amazon S3: approved manual versions
  2. Bedrock Knowledge Bases: synchronize and retrieve relevant passages
  3. Amazon Bedrock: answer using those passages
  4. Response: include and verify source references
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Separate changing knowledge from changing behavior and changing instructions.

Bedrock Knowledge Bases — RAG

Choose when: Answers need external/current evidence with attribution.

Exam trap: RAG still needs current indexes, correct retrieval, and access controls.

Bedrock model customization — fine-tuning

Choose when: An evaluated stable behavior/style need justifies updating supported model weights.

Exam trap: Fine-tuning is not a live document-refresh mechanism.

Bedrock Prompt Management — prompting

Choose when: Instructions, examples, formatting, and reusable templates need refinement.

Exam trap: A template does not fetch missing private facts.

Bedrock response caching

Choose when: Reuse a scoped answer while its evidence and configuration remain valid.

Exam trap: A cache must be invalidated when relevant source versions change.

Managed Knowledge Bases vs. custom RAG

PDF trap 2 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • AWS Lambda
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service
1. Try a multiple-choice question

A team is building an S3-backed assistant with Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Its selected vector store and citation requirements are supported. A document-specific chunking routine can run within the Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation contract. The team needs this routine while minimizing ownership of ingestion and retrieval. The routine preserves section boundaries and adds source metadata; it does not require an unsupported search algorithm. The team can maintain this one Lambda function, but does not want to operate independent index synchronization and citation handling. Which approach should it choose?

  1. Use a Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation for the chunking routine and keep managed embedding, indexing, and retrieval.
  2. Implement the chunking routine in a new Lambda/OpenSearch RAG pipeline and take ownership of synchronization and citations.
  3. Keep default Knowledge Bases ingestion and apply the section-boundary routine to the context after retrieval.
  4. Keep default indexing and increase retrieved context until the document-specific sections are included in the model prompt.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

The custom processing fits a managed extension; the rest of the managed pipeline already meets the requirements.

Why this answer fits

A. Use a Knowledge Bases Lambda transformation for the chunking routine and keep managed embedding, indexing, and retrieval.

Configure custom chunking through the supported Lambda transformation and keep Knowledge Bases responsible for the remaining ingestion and retrieval stages. The requirement is a specific extension, so replacing the entire RAG pipeline would create unnecessary ownership.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Implement the chunking routine in a new Lambda/OpenSearch RAG pipeline and take ownership of synchronization and citations.

    A custom pipeline can perform the routine, but adds synchronization and citation ownership when a supported managed extension meets the stated requirement.

  2. Keep default Knowledge Bases ingestion and apply the section-boundary routine to the context after retrieval.

    Post-retrieval processing cannot change the document units that were embedded, so the required section boundaries are absent from ingestion.

  3. Keep default indexing and increase retrieved context until the document-specific sections are included in the model prompt.

    Larger retrieval context may contain more material, but it does not implement the specified chunking routine and metadata contract.

What would change the answer?

A custom RAG pipeline becomes appropriate when required query, ranking, or ingestion behavior cannot be implemented by the managed service and its supported extensions.

How the services fit together
  1. Amazon S3: document input
  2. AWS Lambda transformation: produce the required chunks
  3. Bedrock Knowledge Bases: embed and index transformed chunks
  4. Knowledge Bases retrieval: supply passages and source references
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Check whether the managed feature meets the requirement before building the whole pipeline.

Knowledge Bases + Lambda transformation

Choose when: Managed RAG features fit, with supported custom chunk/metadata processing.

Exam trap: Managed does not mean automatic entitlement or automatic source freshness.

Custom RAG pipeline

Choose when: Required ranking, query behavior, or stage control is unsupported by managed features.

Exam trap: Custom chunking is not by itself proof that managed RAG cannot fit.

Answer-stage prompt processing

Choose when: Refine how an answer uses evidence already retrieved.

Exam trap: Answer formatting cannot define ingestion-time chunk boundaries.

Expanded retrieval context

Choose when: Additional retrieved passages supply evidence missing from the current context.

Exam trap: More context does not implement custom ingestion-time chunk boundaries.

Embedding dimensions and model fit

PDF trap 7 · Domain 1

Key services and controls
  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2
  • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings G1
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases
1. Try a multiple-choice question

An OpenSearch vector index uses 1,024-dimensional Titan Text Embeddings V2 vectors for documents and queries. Storage cost is increasing. The team wants to evaluate smaller vectors while preserving an agreed retrieval-recall target. The existing index is healthy and a labeled query set establishes the baseline recall. There is no evidence of an ingestion failure. Any new configuration must use a consistent embedding model and vector size for documents and queries. Which plan is technically valid and gives evidence for the decision?

  1. Build 256- and 512-dimensional Titan V2 test indexes with matching query vectors and compare held-out recall and storage.
  2. Switch to 1,536-dimensional Titan G1 vectors for both documents and queries, then migrate after measuring recall.
  3. Keep the 1,024-dimensional document index and issue 256-dimensional query vectors to reduce per-query vector size.
  4. Generate 256-dimensional document and query vectors with Titan V2 and deploy them after confirming indexing succeeds.
Reveal the solutionThe deciding clue

Reduce vector size while keeping document and query embeddings compatible and measuring retrieval quality.

Why this answer fits

A. Build 256- and 512-dimensional Titan V2 test indexes with matching query vectors and compare held-out recall and storage.

Titan V2 supports 256, 512, and 1,024 dimensions. Build separate compatible test indexes for the smaller configurations and use matching query vectors on the same held-out questions. Compare recall and storage before selecting a configuration; vector size alone does not establish quality.

Why the alternatives fail
  1. Switch to 1,536-dimensional Titan G1 vectors for both documents and queries, then migrate after measuring recall.

    G1 is a different embedding model and its larger vectors do not meet the stated smaller-vector storage objective.

  2. Keep the 1,024-dimensional document index and issue 256-dimensional query vectors to reduce per-query vector size.

    The query vectors cannot be compared with the existing document vectors at a different dimension.

  3. Generate 256-dimensional document and query vectors with Titan V2 and deploy them after confirming indexing succeeds.

    The dimensions are supported and compatible, but indexing success does not establish that the required recall target is preserved.

What would change the answer?

If smaller vectors fail the recall target, retain the higher-dimensional configuration or evaluate other embedding and retrieval choices on the same test set.

How the services fit together
  1. Held-out questions: define the recall target
  2. Titan V2: create matching document and query vectors
  3. OpenSearch test indexes: compare 256 / 512 / 1,024 dimensions
  4. Decision: select a configuration that meets quality and cost targets
Read the related guide →
2. Learn the distinction

Compare quality and cost within the actual embedding model contract; dimensions are not an accuracy guarantee.

Titan V2 supported dimensions

Choose when: Choose among supported V2 dimensions using workload measurements.

Exam trap: Lower dimensions can affect quality; storage savings are not the whole bill.

Titan G1 embeddings

Choose when: Evaluate a different embedding model with a compatible rebuilt corpus and query path.
